claims.text: The undoped Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification.
The undoped alloy undergoes a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1 at.% Zr to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Zr atoms will segregate to microscopic nucleation sites in the melt or glassy matrix.
Zr will preferentially segregate to incipient crystalline clusters and potential nucleation sites.
Segregation of Zr will increase the activation-energy barrier for crystal nucleation.
The increased nucleation barrier will suppress primary non-eutectic crystalline-phase formation.
Zr doping will delay crystallization during cooling.
Zr doping will delay crystallization during reheating.
Relative to the undoped alloy, Zr doping will expand the cooling-rate window for glass formation.
Relative to the undoped alloy, Zr doping will increase the retained amorphous fraction.
During reheating, the Zr-doped alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the undoped alloy.
Zr doping will improve the alloy's thermal stability.
Zr doping will significantly reduce extensive primary crystallization.
The undoped alloy fully crystallizes at slower cooling rates.
The intervention is intended to remain effective during rapid cooling, slower cooling, and subsequent controlled reheating.

contradictions.description: The conditions describe rapid cooling as being beyond a critical rate for full nucleation of crystalline phases, whereas the boundary describes cooling above the critical threshold as normally bypassing full crystallization. These assign opposite meanings to crossing the critical cooling-rate threshold.

The baseline broadly states that extensive primary crystallization occurs even under varying cooling rates, while the boundary states that sufficiently rapid cooling normally bypasses full crystallization. The applicable rapid-cooling behavior is therefore internally ambiguous.
